text.en: Have you ever looked up at the sky and noticed that it never looks the same? In the morning it can be orange, at noon the sunlight is strong and at night the Moon and stars appear. In this chapter you will watch the Sun on its journey, find out why shadows change, learn how the Moon changes shape, and see how festivals follow the Moon.

The sky looks different at different times of the day. Its colour changes in the morning, the afternoon and the night, and the Sun's colour seems to change too. The size and shape of the Moon also seem to change over time. The activities of birds, animals, trees and people change during the day as well. In the morning the sky can look orange and the Sun looks orange. In the afternoon the sunlight is strong. At night we can see the Moon and stars. You can draw three pictures of the sky, morning, afternoon and night, and write a table of what you notice in each.
The brightest object in the sky is the Sun. It is so bright that other stars cannot be seen when the Sun is in the sky. The Sun gives us light and heat. The Sun appears to rise in the morning, move up until it is overhead, and then slowly go down on the other side until it disappears. We all enjoy this visible journey of the Sun across the sky. At sunrise the sky is bright and orange, birds start to chirp and fly out, people wake up and the day begins at home. At sunset the sky turns red and orange, birds return to their nests, and at home we switch on lights and the day winds down.
A shadow forms when an object blocks light. Your shadow moves along with you, and if you make different poses its shape changes. Shadows in the morning are long, shadows at noon are short, and shadows in the evening are long again. Evening shadows point in the opposite direction to morning shadows. Shadows form only when something stops light, so they need a source of light like the Sun or a torch.
Take a torch and a stick and make the room dark. Hold the stick in one place and shine the torch on it. If the stick is close to the torch, the shadow is bigger. If you move it away, the shadow becomes smaller. If you change the direction of the torch, the direction of the shadow changes too. This explains the Sun: as the Sun appears to move across the sky, the direction and length of shadows change.
The Sun appears to move from the East in the morning to overhead at noon and then towards the West in the afternoon. When the Sun is low in the East, the shadow falls long towards the West. At noon, with the Sun overhead, the shadow is short. In the evening the Sun is low in the West, so the shadow falls long towards the East. So the direction of a shadow changes because of the apparent movement of the Sun.
Ancient people noticed that shadows change through the day and made a device called a sundial to tell the time. Raja Jai Singh of Jaipur built Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, Ujjain, Delhi, Varanasi and Mathura. It has a huge sundial called Samrat Yantra, which can tell the time accurately from the shadow. Shadow puppetry has been practised in India for a long time, and you can play with shadows by making animal shapes with your hands.
After sunset the sky is full of thousands of twinkling stars, and we can see patterns of stars in the night sky. Some patterns have names, like Saptarshi, the Seven Sages, but any pattern you see is worth drawing. The Moon appears to be the biggest object in the night sky and has always fascinated people. Sky watching is a good habit: look at the sky at the same time every night and keep notes.
The Moon looks different on different nights. On some nights it is a complete circle, called Poornima or the full Moon. On other nights it looks like the letter C, or as if it has been cut in half. On some nights it is not visible at all, which is called Amavasya or the new Moon. This cycle repeats, so people in ancient cultures used the shape of the Moon to count days, and this gave rise to the earliest calendars. Diwali is celebrated when there is no Moon in the sky. Rakshabandhan, Guru Poornima and Buddha Poornima are celebrated when the full Moon is visible. Eid is celebrated on the first night the Moon is seen after the new Moon. Pongal, Chhath Puja and Karva Chauth are other festivals linked to the Sun or the Moon. On 23 August 2023 India's Vikram Lander landed successfully on the Moon as part of the Chandrayaan mission and collected data about the Moon's surface.

problem.en: Where will your shadow fall in the morning, if the Sun is in the East?

text.en: In the morning the Sun is low in the East.

why.en: The Sun is on the East side.

text.en: A shadow falls on the side opposite to the Sun.

why.en: The object blocks the light from the Sun.

text.en: So the shadow falls towards the West.

why.en: In the evening the Sun is in the West and the shadow falls to the East.

problem.en: Why is your shadow shorter at noon than in the morning?

text.en: At noon the Sun is high overhead.

why.en: The light comes almost from above.

text.en: When light comes from above, the shadow falls close under the object.
In the morning the Sun is low and the shadow stretches far.

why.en: So noon shadows are the shortest.

prompt.en: Explain how the Sun appears to move and how that changes shadows during the day.

requiredIdeas.en: Sun rises in the East, overhead at noon, sets in the West
Morning shadow is long and points West
Evening shadow is long and points East

commonMisconceptions.en: The Sun does not move at all

points.en: The Sun is the brightest object in the sky and gives light and heat.
Shadows are long in the morning and evening and short at noon.
The direction of a shadow changes as the Sun appears to move from East to West.
The Moon changes shape in a cycle, and people used it to make calendars.
Many festivals follow the Sun or the Moon.
